title: Implement a Contact Centre as a Service
context: We use a legacy application, on-prem, unsupported that cover VOIP.
problem: It doesn't support where the business needs to be
proposal: We want to implement a full CCaaS platform that covers all digital platforms and channels of communication, to drive customer engagement, interface with CRM and feed the work planning.
narrative:
## Context

We use a legacy application, on-prem, unsupported that cover VOIP.

## Problem

It doesn't support where the business needs to be

## Proposal

We want to implement a full CCaaS platform that covers all digital platforms and channels of communication, to drive customer engagement, interface with CRM and feed the work planning.

requirements.statement: Support omnichannel customer communication across voice, email, chat, and SMS channels.
Interface with the CRM system to capture customer context and enrich interactions.
Feed contact centre interactions to the work planning system to create and update work queue items.
Support a minimum of 500 concurrent contact centre agents.
Achieve end-to-end integration latency with CRM and work planning systems of less than 5 seconds.

recommendations.recommendation: **Clarify the problem statement.** The context 'unsupported' legacy VOIP system is clear, but the problem statement 'It doesn't support where the business needs to be' is vague. Add concrete pain points — e.g. *lacks email and chat capabilities needed for modern customer engagement, cannot route to specialist queues, cannot track customer context across channels*. This will help stakeholders and architects understand the true business constraint.

**Define 'CCaaS' for a business audience.** The narrative uses the acronym without explanation. Add a sentence explaining that CCaaS means *a cloud-based contact centre platform managed by an external vendor, reducing on-premises infrastructure and support burden*. This ensures the decision is accessible to business readers without technical knowledge.

**Enumerate the digital channels explicitly.** The narrative mentions 'all digital platforms and channels' and the requirements now specify voice, email, chat, SMS — good progress. Consider clarifying in the narrative whether social media (Facebook, Twitter, etc.) is in scope, and whether all channels will be available from day one or phased.

**Clarify the strategic motivation.** Link the CCaaS decision explicitly to the business strategy already in the decision JSON — the narrative should state that this platform enables 'customer-centric operations' and supports the goal of '90% of frontline staff in cross-functional customer-facing teams by 2027'. This elevates the initiative from a technology refresh to a strategic capability enabler.

impact-assessment.finding: The decision proposes adopting a **Contact Centre as a Service (CCaaS)** platform to replace a legacy on-premises VOIP application. This is a strategic acquisition of a new application capability covering omnichannel communication.
impact-assessment.impact: The Application Catalogue (`APP-CAT`) will require a new entry for the CCaaS vendor product. The Application Domains & Platforms (`APP-DAP`) may need a new platform grouping to organize CCaaS and related capabilities. Without updating these artefacts, the new application will be invisible to architecture views and impact analysis.
impact-assessment.recommendation: **Add** a new entry to the **Application Catalogue** (`APP-CAT`) with the CCaaS product name, vendor, and lifecycle status. Determine whether **Application Domains & Platforms** (`APP-DAP`) requires a new platform grouping to represent the CCaaS solution, and **add** or **update** it accordingly.
impact-assessment.rationale: The physical application layer (`APP-CAT`) is the single source of truth for deployed systems. The logical platform layer (`APP-DAP`) determines how capabilities are organized across the application landscape. Capturing the CCaaS platform ensures visibility in downstream architecture models and enables impact analysis on dependent systems.

impact-assessment.finding: The narrative states the CCaaS platform will 'drive customer engagement, interface with CRM and feed the work planning.' This indicates new integrations with at least two external systems (CRM and work planning), plus inbound customer engagement flows.
impact-assessment.impact: The Interface Catalogue (`INT-IFC`) will need new interface definitions for: CCaaS ↔ CRM synchronization, CCaaS ↔ work planning system, and possibly inbound customer engagement channels. Without these definitions, the integration landscape will be incomplete and integration governance will lack enforcement points.
impact-assessment.recommendation: **Add** entries to the **Interface Catalogue** (`INT-IFC`) for each integration point: CCaaS to CRM, CCaaS to work planning, and any bidirectional customer engagement flows. Document the direction of data flow and the conceptual entities crossing each interface (via **Data Domains & Concepts ↔ Interface Catalogue** (`INT-DAC-IFC`)).
impact-assessment.rationale: The Interface Catalogue is the authoritative definition of system-to-system connections. Interfaces must be recorded before implementation to ensure data governance, performance contracts, and integration standards are applied consistently across the landscape.

impact-assessment.finding: The decision mentions that the CCaaS platform will interface with CRM and work planning, but does not specify what data entities are involved, their CRUD operations, or ownership. The narrative lacks clarity on data governance and data flow direction.
impact-assessment.impact: The Data Domains & Concepts (`DAT-DAC`) may require new data entities if the CCaaS platform owns or creates new data (e.g. contact centre interaction records, queue state). The Process-to-Data CRUD matrix (`DAT-PRO-DAC`) will need updates to reflect which business processes create/read/update/delete data flowing through the CCaaS platform. Downstream applications consuming work queue updates from the CCaaS cannot be validated without this clarity.
impact-assessment.recommendation: **Review and clarify** the data governance boundaries: which entities does CCaaS create, read, update, or own? **Update** or **add** entries to **Data Domains & Concepts** (`DAT-DAC`) if new data subject areas are introduced. **Update** the **Process ↔ Data CRUD matrix** (`DAT-PRO-DAC`) to reflect the CCaaS platform's role in data flows, particularly for customer interaction records and work queue updates.
impact-assessment.rationale: Data governance is a precondition for sound architecture. Mapping data entities to the processes that use them, and to the systems that own them, prevents data quality issues and ensures the CCaaS platform integrates cleanly with the organisation's data management practices.

impact-assessment.finding: The decision's narrative provides insufficient clarity on scope. It does not enumerate specific communication channels (phone, email, chat, SMS, social media), identify which channels replace legacy VOIP, which are new, or define the target customer segments. Requirements are absent.
impact-assessment.impact: Without clear requirements and scope boundaries, architecture analysis cannot determine whether capabilities in the Business Capabilities (`BUS-CAP`) catalogue require updates, whether business processes must be remodelled, or whether the CCaaS platform introduces process innovations that should be captured in the Business Processes (`BUS-PRO`) catalogue. This creates risk of scope creep and misalignment between business intent and technical delivery.
impact-assessment.recommendation: **Before proceeding**, clarify the business scope: enumerate the digital channels and customer segments in scope; state which capabilities (from `BUS-CAP`) the CCaaS platform enables or enhances; and confirm whether business processes must be updated to reflect omnichannel customer engagement workflows. Once scope is clear, **review and update** `BUS-CAP` and `BUS-PRO` as needed.
impact-assessment.rationale: The Business Capabilities and Processes catalogues are the business's formal architecture view. Aligning the CCaaS initiative to these artefacts ensures the decision is grounded in business strategy and that downstream architecture work (application platforms, integration, data) flows logically from business intent.

impact-assessment.finding: The decision does not reference any applicable strategies, principles, or guardrails from the cross-domain baseline artefacts (e.g. **Application Architecture Strategy** (`APP-STR`), **Application Architecture Principles** (`APP-PRN`), **Integration Architecture Guardrails** (`INT-GRD`)).
impact-assessment.impact: The absence of explicit traceability to governance standards creates risk that the CCaaS platform may be implemented without applying relevant constraints on integration patterns, data protection, vendor lock-in, or operational resilience. Downstream decision-makers will lack clear guidance on how to operationalize this decision within the governance framework.
impact-assessment.recommendation: **Review** the existing **Application Architecture Strategy** (`APP-STR`), **Principles** (`APP-PRN`), **Guardrails** (`APP-GRD`), **Integration Principles** (`INT-PRN`), and **Integration Guardrails** (`INT-GRD`). Explicitly state which of these apply to the CCaaS platform in the ADR narrative. If no applicable strategy or principle exists, this signals a governance gap that may need to be addressed in a separate decision.
impact-assessment.rationale: Architecture governance is enforced through explicit strategy and principles. Tracing the CCaaS initiative to these foundational artefacts ensures the platform operates within the organisation's risk tolerance, vendor standards, and technical constraints.

strategy-alignment.finding: The decision to adopt a **Contact Centre as a Service (CCaaS)** platform directly advances **Application Strategy** (`APP-STR`) statement *'Buy or assemble for commodity capability; build only where it differentiates'* (APP-STR-002). Contact centre management is a commodity capability; acquiring CCaaS rather than building internally aligns with the target of reducing custom-build share below 40% by 2027.
strategy-alignment.impact: This decision strengthens the business case by demonstrating adherence to the buy-vs-build strategy. It frees internal engineering capacity to focus on differentiating capabilities and reduces ongoing maintenance burden on a non-strategic system.
strategy-alignment.recommendation: Explicitly reference APP-STR-002 in the ADR narrative to establish the strategic rationale. When evaluating CCaaS vendors, evaluate them against the criterion of commodity interchangeability — ensure the chosen platform is not vendor-locked in ways that would constrain future replacement.
strategy-alignment.rationale: The portfolio strategy hinges on protecting engineering capacity for competitive differentiation. A commodity CCaaS acquisition is strategically aligned with this priority and should be highlighted to stakeholders as evidence of disciplined application portfolio management.

strategy-alignment.finding: The decision advances **Business Strategy** (`BUS-STR`) statement *'Operate as a customer-centric organisation, organised around end-to-end customer outcomes'* (BUS-STR-001). The CCaaS platform enables omnichannel customer engagement across digital channels, directly supporting the target of 90% of frontline staff in cross-functional customer-facing teams by end of 2027.
strategy-alignment.impact: The CCaaS platform is an enabling capability for customer-centric operations. Implementing it removes a technical barrier to the business goal of NPS improvement and cross-functional customer engagement, thereby increasing the confidence in meeting the 2027 outcome.
strategy-alignment.recommendation: Link the CCaaS initiative to the BUS-STR-001 outcome explicitly. Confirm with business stakeholders that the omnichannel capability set (phone, email, chat, SMS, social) aligns with the frontline channels they expect their customer-facing teams to operate through. Document this alignment in the requirements.
strategy-alignment.rationale: Strategic buy-in is critical for investment funding and prioritisation. Explicitly connecting the CCaaS initiative to a named strategic outcome (NPS improvement, customer-facing team structure) elevates the decision beyond a technology refresh to a strategic capability enabler.

strategy-alignment.finding: The decision has a positive but unclear relationship to **Data Strategy** (`DAT-STR`) statement *'Treat data as a product — each domain publishes data assets consumed by the rest of the business'* (DAT-STR-001). The narrative mentions CCaaS will 'feed the work planning' and interface with CRM, implying data flows, but does not define what data entities the CCaaS platform will publish or own.
strategy-alignment.impact: The absence of clarity on data ownership creates a risk that contact centre interaction data (a valuable asset for business analytics) will not be managed as a formal data product. This may result in shadow analytics or repeated custom pipelines rather than the self-serve data products the strategy envisions.
strategy-alignment.recommendation: Define which entities the CCaaS platform will publish as data products — e.g. 'contact centre interaction records', 'queue state', 'agent availability' — and confirm these are owned by the CCaaS domain and published per the DAT-STR-001 approach. Ensure the CRM and work planning integrations are documented in the Data Domains & Concepts (`DAT-DAC`) catalogue as data product consumers.
strategy-alignment.rationale: Data strategy success depends on clarity about which system owns each data entity. The CCaaS platform will generate valuable customer interaction data; explicitly committing this to the data-as-a-product model ensures it supports organisational decision-making and avoids siloed analytics.

strategy-alignment.finding: The decision strongly advances **Integration Strategy** (`INT-STR`) statement *'API-first: every new inter-system exchange is a versioned, managed API by default'* (INT-STR-001) and *'Contract-first: API and event schemas are designed and reviewed before implementation begins'* (INT-STR-003). The CCaaS platform integrations with CRM and work planning should be API-first with managed contracts.
strategy-alignment.impact: The CCaaS platform is positioned as a source of inter-system exchanges (state changes in contact centre work queues, customer interactions, agent availability). Implementing these as managed APIs with contract-first design aligns with the integration strategy and positions the platform as a reusable capability per INT-STR-005.
strategy-alignment.recommendation: In the ADR narrative, explicitly state that CCaaS integrations with CRM and work planning will use versioned, managed APIs with contract-first design. Define the integration contracts in the **Interface Catalogue** (`INT-IFC`) before vendor selection or implementation. Reference INT-STR-001 and INT-STR-003 as the strategic drivers.
strategy-alignment.rationale: Integration debt is a major constraint on new initiatives (est. 40% of new-initiative effort). Establishing API-first contracts upfront prevents tight coupling, ensures integrations can be reused by future initiatives, and makes the platform disposable if business needs change.

strategy-alignment.finding: The decision's alignment with **Application Strategy** (`APP-STR`) statement *'Cloud-native first — every new application is designed for the cloud operating model'* (APP-STR-001) is silent. The narrative does not state whether the CCaaS platform will be cloud-native or on-premises, nor whether it will support observability and continuous delivery.
strategy-alignment.impact: Absent clarity on cloud-native operating model and observability, the CCaaS platform may become a long-term operational liability. If the vendor platform does not support cloud-native patterns or observability, it will diverge from the baseline expectation and create operational friction.
strategy-alignment.recommendation: Clarify in the ADR narrative whether the chosen CCaaS vendor platform is cloud-native (containers, immutable infrastructure, declarative deployment) and supports the observability requirements of APP-STR-005 (logs, metrics, traces). If the vendor platform does not support these, explicitly acknowledge the divergence and document a mitigation strategy.
strategy-alignment.rationale: The organisation's application baseline is shifting toward cloud-native, containerised services with standard observability. A CCaaS platform that does not align with these expectations will require custom integration for observability and may not support continuous deployment practices, creating technical debt.

principles-alignment.finding: **Application Principles** (`APP-PRN`) principle *'Twelve-factor app methodology'* (`APP-PRN-001`) is **silent**. The narrative does not state whether the CCaaS vendor platform follows twelve-factor patterns (config via environment, stateless processes, port-binding, stdout logging).
principles-alignment.impact: If the CCaaS platform does not follow twelve-factor patterns, deployment, scaling, and portability will be constrained. The organisation's baseline assumption is that applications are cloud-native and portable; a vendor platform that violates this creates operational friction and may lock the organisation into that vendor's deployment model.
principles-alignment.recommendation: During vendor evaluation, confirm that the CCaaS platform is twelve-factor compliant — specifically, that configuration is externalised to environment variables, processes are stateless, and logs are written to stdout for platform aggregation. If the vendor platform deviates, explicitly acknowledge the deviation and document a mitigation strategy (e.g. wrapper containerisation).
principles-alignment.rationale: Twelve-factor patterns are the foundational contract for cloud-native operations. They enable rapid scaling, immutable deployments, and platform portability. A CCaaS platform that does not meet these expectations will require custom integration for logging and scaling, creating technical debt.

principles-alignment.finding: **Application Principles** (`APP-PRN`) principle *'Composable over monolithic'* (`APP-PRN-002`) is **silent**. The narrative does not state whether the CCaaS platform will be consumed as a service or integrated as a monolithic system.
principles-alignment.impact: If the CCaaS platform is integrated as a tightly coupled monolith (rather than exposing capabilities via stable, versioned interfaces), teams consuming CCaaS capabilities will be locked into the vendor's release cycle and unable to evolve their processes independently.
principles-alignment.recommendation: In the ADR narrative, clarify that the CCaaS platform will publish its contact centre capabilities (e.g. call routing, queue management, agent assignment) via stable, versioned APIs. Ensure these APIs are documented in the **Interface Catalogue** (`INT-IFC`) before vendor selection, and confirm that the chosen vendor's APIs meet the stability and versioning expectations of `APP-PRN-002`.
principles-alignment.rationale: Composability is critical for team autonomy and independent evolution. A CCaaS platform that exposes its capabilities only through internal integrations or proprietary connectors will create a new technical bottleneck, contradicting the principle that services should be independently replaceable.

principles-alignment.finding: **Application Principles** (`APP-PRN`) principle *'Observability is built in, not bolted on'* (`APP-PRN-005`) is **silent**. The narrative does not confirm that the CCaaS platform will expose health, structured logs, RED metrics, and distributed traces compatible with the organisation's observability stack.
principles-alignment.impact: If the CCaaS platform does not emit standard observability signals (logs, metrics, traces), operations teams will lack visibility into CCaaS performance and failures. This will impair incident response and create operational blind spots, violating the principle that observability is a first-class design quality.
principles-alignment.recommendation: Document in the ADR narrative that the chosen CCaaS vendor platform will emit logs, metrics (requests/errors/duration), and traces in standard formats consumable by the organisation's observability platform (e.g. OpenTelemetry, CloudWatch, Datadog). If the vendor platform does not support standard observability, clarify the workaround (e.g. sidecar collectors, vendor-native integration).
principles-alignment.rationale: Observability is essential for operational resilience. The organisation's baseline assumption is that every service exposes health and telemetry from day one. A CCaaS platform that requires custom instrumentation or offers only vendor-proprietary telemetry will slow incident response and fragment the observability estate.

principles-alignment.finding: **Integration Principles** (`INT-PRN`) principle *'Contracts before code'* (`INT-PRN-002`) is **violated**. The narrative proposes that the CCaaS platform will 'interface with CRM and feed the work planning' but does not define the API contracts, schemas, or integration boundaries before vendor selection or implementation. No contracts are documented in the **Interface Catalogue** (`INT-IFC`).
principles-alignment.impact: Without contract-first design, the integration will be driven by the CCaaS vendor's API shape and internal models. This will leak vendor-specific concerns into the organisation's integration landscape, make it harder to replace the CCaaS vendor later, and increase the risk of tight coupling between CCaaS and consuming systems (CRM, work planning).
principles-alignment.recommendation: **Before vendor selection**, define the integration contracts between CCaaS and CRM, and between CCaaS and work planning. Document these contracts in the **Interface Catalogue** (`INT-IFC`) using OpenAPI 3.0 (for synchronous APIs) or AsyncAPI 3.0 (for event-driven flows). Specify the entities crossing each interface, the direction of data flow, and the SLAs (latency, availability). Use these contracts to evaluate vendors, and reject vendors whose APIs do not align with the contracted schema.
principles-alignment.rationale: Contract-first design is the foundation of loose coupling and vendor portability. Integrations driven by vendor APIs lock the organisation into implementation details that become expensive to change. By designing contracts first, the organisation retains control over the integration shape and can swap vendors without rewriting consuming systems.

principles-alignment.finding: **Integration Principles** (`INT-PRN`) principle *'Internal model does not leak into the integration model'* (`INT-PRN-006`) is **at risk**. The narrative does not define how contact centre concepts (e.g. 'agent', 'queue', 'interaction') will be translated from the CCaaS vendor's internal model into shared domain language before being published to CRM and work planning systems.
principles-alignment.impact: If the CCaaS platform publishes vendor-internal data structures (e.g. proprietary agent IDs, vendor-specific queue formats) directly to downstream systems, the organisation's integration landscape will become tightly coupled to the CCaaS vendor. Replacing the vendor will require rewriting integrations in consuming systems.
principles-alignment.recommendation: In the ADR narrative, clarify that the CCaaS platform will translate vendor-internal models to shared domain concepts at the integration boundary. Define these concepts in the **Data Domains & Concepts** (`DAT-DAC`) catalogue (e.g. 'Contact Centre Interaction', 'Agent Assignment', 'Queue State'). Ensure the **Interface Catalogue** (`INT-IFC`) expresses these shared concepts, not vendor-internal structures.
principles-alignment.rationale: Leaked internal models are a primary source of integration debt. By translating vendor concepts to shared domain language at the boundary, the organisation decouples from the vendor's implementation and preserves the ability to replace the CCaaS platform later without rewriting downstream systems.

principles-alignment.finding: **Data Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) principle *'Every data domain has an owner'* (`DAT-PRN-001`) is **silent**. The narrative does not identify an owner or steward for the contact centre data domain (interaction records, queue state, agent availability) that the CCaaS platform will produce.
principles-alignment.impact: Without a named owner for contact centre data, quality governance is diffuse and accountability unclear. Data quality issues, definition drift, and lifecycle decisions (e.g. retention, deletion) will lack clear ownership, creating risk that the valuable contact centre data asset will be poorly managed.
principles-alignment.recommendation: Identify and name the data steward responsible for contact centre data produced by the CCaaS platform (e.g. 'Contact Centre Operations Manager', 'Data Owner: Customer Engagement'). Document this ownership decision in the ADR narrative and ensure it is reflected in the **Data Domains & Concepts** (`DAT-DAC`) catalogue when contact centre data entities are added.
principles-alignment.rationale: Data ownership is the precondition for governance. Unowned data drifts in quality and meaning. By assigning clear stewardship of contact centre data, the organisation ensures data quality is monitored, definitions are maintained, and lifecycle decisions are made with accountability.

principles-alignment.finding: **Data Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) principle *'Define once, use everywhere'* (`DAT-PRN-002`) is **at risk**. The narrative does not reference or align with existing data concepts in the **Data Domains & Concepts** (`DAT-DAC`) catalogue. If contact centre concepts (e.g. 'customer interaction', 'agent', 'queue') already exist in DAT-DAC, the CCaaS platform must use the same definitions rather than creating parallel ones.
principles-alignment.impact: If the CCaaS platform defines contact centre concepts independently of existing data domains, the organisation will have multiple conflicting definitions of the same concept across systems. This creates silent divergence, undermines analytics, and produces inconsistent data products.
principles-alignment.recommendation: Before CCaaS vendor selection or requirements definition, review the **Data Domains & Concepts** (`DAT-DAC`) catalogue to identify any existing definitions for contact centre entities (e.g. 'Customer Interaction', 'Contact Channel'). If they exist, ensure the CCaaS platform aligns with them. If they do not, add them to DAT-DAC (with a named owner) before the CCaaS platform begins implementation, and ensure the vendor's data model conforms to these canonical definitions.
principles-alignment.rationale: Canonical definitions are the foundation of trustworthy cross-domain analysis. By ensuring the CCaaS platform uses the same definitions as the rest of the organisation, analytics teams can join contact centre data with customer, CRM, and operational data without manual reconciliation.

principles-alignment.finding: **Data Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) principle *'Privacy by design'* (`DAT-PRN-004`) is **at risk**. The narrative does not address how personal data (customer phone numbers, email addresses, interaction transcripts) will be classified, consent-tracked, and access-controlled within the CCaaS platform and in downstream integrations with CRM and work planning.
principles-alignment.impact: Contact centre interactions are inherently personal data (customer contact details, interaction content, agent notes). If privacy controls are not designed into the CCaaS platform from day one, the organisation risks compliance violations, data breaches, and difficulty enforcing consent and access rules across CRM and work planning systems consuming CCaaS data.
principles-alignment.recommendation: In the ADR narrative, explicitly state that the CCaaS platform will classify personal data fields at capture time, enforce consent tracking and access controls at query time, and support anonymisation for analytics use cases. Confirm that the chosen CCaaS vendor provides APIs for classification, consent, and access control. Document these requirements in the vendor evaluation criteria and ensure they are part of the integration contract in **Interface Catalogue** (`INT-IFC`).
principles-alignment.rationale: Privacy retrofitted onto established data flows is expensive and incomplete. The CCaaS platform will be a primary source of customer personal data; designing privacy controls from day one ensures compliance with regulations (GDPR, CCPA) and operational resilience.

principles-alignment.finding: **Business Principles** (`BUS-PRN`) principle *'Customer journey as the unit of design'* (`BUS-PRN-005`) is **partially adhered to**. The narrative acknowledges that CCaaS will 'drive customer engagement' and support 'omnichannel communication', which are customer-centric motivations. However, it does not identify the specific customer journeys the CCaaS platform will enable or improve.
principles-alignment.impact: Without clear mapping to customer journeys, it is unclear how the CCaaS platform integrates into end-to-end customer experience processes. This risks siloed implementation where the CCaaS platform is optimised for operations rather than customer outcomes, and creates difficulty in measuring impact on customer satisfaction and NPS.
principles-alignment.recommendation: In the ADR narrative, identify the customer journeys that CCaaS will enable or improve — e.g. 'Customer Reports an Issue → Contact Centre → Resolution → Follow-up'. Confirm that the CCaaS platform's capabilities (omnichannel contact, routing, queue management) are designed to support these journeys end-to-end, not just internal operations. Reference these journeys in the **Business Processes** (`BUS-PRO`) catalogue and ensure downstream architecture (application, data, integration) traces back to customer outcomes.
principles-alignment.rationale: Customer-centric design ensures the CCaaS investment creates external value, not just internal efficiency. By mapping the platform to named customer journeys, the organisation ensures architecture decisions (e.g. channel prioritisation, routing algorithms) are aligned with customer outcomes rather than operational convenience.

principles-alignment.finding: **Business Principles** (`BUS-PRN`) principle *'Process digital by default'* (`BUS-PRN-006`) is **partially adhered to**. The CCaaS platform is inherently digital (cloud-based contact centre as a service), and the narrative suggests it will replace a legacy on-premises VOIP system. However, the narrative does not clarify whether the digital contact centre processes will be end-to-end without manual steps, or whether manual workarounds will remain in the customer engagement workflow.
principles-alignment.impact: If the contact centre workflow includes manual steps (e.g. manual queue assignment, manual customer routing rules, manual escalation), the organisation will not realise the full benefits of the digital CCaaS platform (speed, auditability, measurability). Additionally, manual steps create operational brittleness and limit the foundation for future AI-assisted operations.
principles-alignment.recommendation: In the ADR narrative, clarify that the CCaaS platform's customer engagement and internal workflows will be fully digital end-to-end. If specific manual steps are necessary (e.g. complex escalations, special handling), document them with a remediation plan to automate them within a defined timeframe. Ensure the **Business Processes** (`BUS-PRO`) catalogue reflects fully digital workflows for contact centre operations.
principles-alignment.rationale: Digital-by-default execution is the only basis for measurable outcomes and AI-assisted operations. If manual steps remain in the contact centre workflow, the organisation will have incomplete data for analytics and lack the foundation for future intelligent automation.

guardrails-alignment.finding: **Business Guardrails** (`BUS-GRD`) catalogue is empty — no guardrails are currently defined.
guardrails-alignment.impact: Without guardrail definitions, the decision cannot be assessed for compliance with business-level constraints (e.g. regulatory, operational, compliance, risk-management rules). The absence of guardrails in the baseline creates governance blind spots and prevents enforcement of business standards on architecture decisions.
guardrails-alignment.recommendation: **Populate the Business Guardrails (`BUS-GRD`) catalogue before finalising this decision.** Define guardrails that address business-level risks relevant to the CCaaS initiative — e.g. data residency, regulatory compliance (GDPR, CCPA), customer privacy, audit and compliance reporting, vendor lock-in, and operational resilience. Once guardrails are defined, re-run guardrails alignment to validate this decision against them.
guardrails-alignment.rationale: Guardrails are the organisation's top-level control framework. A CCaaS platform that will handle customer personal data and integrate with CRM requires explicit business-level guardrails to ensure compliance, privacy, and operational governance are achieved.

guardrails-alignment.finding: **Application Guardrails** (`APP-GRD`) catalogue is empty — no guardrails are currently defined.
guardrails-alignment.impact: Without application-level guardrails, the decision cannot be assessed for compliance with constraints on cloud deployment, vendor selection, licensing, support models, or operational standards (e.g. uptime SLAs, incident response, observability, data backup). The CCaaS platform will be implemented without explicit architectural guardrails.
guardrails-alignment.recommendation: **Populate the Application Guardrails (`APP-GRD`) catalogue before finalising this decision.** Define guardrails that address application-level risks — e.g. cloud-first and cloud-only deployments, supported vendor ecosystems, licensing and cost controls, observability and telemetry standards, incident response time targets, and backup/disaster recovery requirements. Once defined, re-run guardrails alignment to validate the CCaaS platform against these guardrails.
guardrails-alignment.rationale: Application guardrails enforce technical standards across the portfolio. A CCaaS platform is a new, external system that will become part of the operational landscape; explicit guardrails ensure the vendor meets the organisation's standards for uptime, observability, compliance, and operational support.

guardrails-alignment.finding: **Integration Guardrails** (`INT-GRD`) catalogue is empty — no guardrails are currently defined.
guardrails-alignment.impact: Without integration-level guardrails, the decision cannot be assessed for compliance with constraints on API design, data exchange security, integration patterns, or contract governance. The CCaaS integrations with CRM and work planning will be built without explicit integration standards.
guardrails-alignment.recommendation: **Populate the Integration Guardrails (`INT-GRD`) catalogue before finalising this decision.** Define guardrails that address integration risks — e.g. API versioning and lifecycle management, encryption-in-transit and data exchange security, API rate limiting and quota controls, integration monitoring and alerting, and contract-first design requirements. Once defined, re-run guardrails alignment to validate the proposed CCaaS integrations against these guardrails.
guardrails-alignment.rationale: Integration guardrails prevent tight coupling and ensure integration debt does not accumulate. The CCaaS platform will establish new inter-system exchanges with CRM and work planning; explicit guardrails ensure these integrations are loosely coupled, monitored, and standards-compliant.

guardrails-alignment.finding: **Data Guardrails** (`DAT-GRD`) catalogue is empty — no guardrails are currently defined.
guardrails-alignment.impact: Without data-level guardrails, the decision cannot be assessed for compliance with constraints on data classification, privacy (GDPR, CCPA), retention, deletion, access control, or data quality standards. The CCaaS platform will produce customer personal data without explicit data governance guardrails.
guardrails-alignment.recommendation: **Populate the Data Guardrails (`DAT-GRD`) catalogue before finalising this decision.** Define guardrails that address data governance risks — e.g. data classification and labelling standards, personal data protection and consent management, retention and deletion policies, access control requirements, and data quality SLAs. Once defined, re-run guardrails alignment to validate the CCaaS data governance model against these guardrails.
guardrails-alignment.rationale: Data guardrails are essential for privacy compliance and risk management. A CCaaS platform will handle customer contact details, interaction transcripts, and agent notes (all personal data); explicit guardrails ensure privacy controls, consent tracking, and compliance are designed in from day one.

referential-integrity.finding: All referential integrity checks passed for the architecture catalogues in scope.
referential-integrity.impact: The existing **Application Catalogue** (`APP-CAT`), **Application Domains & Platforms** (`APP-DAP`), **Interface Catalogue** (`INT-IFC`), **Data Domains & Concepts ↔ Interface Catalogue** (`INT-DAC-IFC`), **Data Domains & Concepts** (`DAT-DAC`), **Process-to-Data CRUD matrix** (`DAT-PRO-DAC`), and **Business Processes** (`BUS-PRO`) catalogues all maintain referential integrity. No broken foreign keys, orphaned entities, or ID uniqueness violations were detected.
referential-integrity.recommendation: No corrective action required. When the CCaaS decision moves to implementation, ensure that any new application, interface, data concept, or process entries added to the catalogues maintain referential integrity by correctly linking to their parent entities and validating all foreign key references before committing changes.
referential-integrity.rationale: Referential integrity is the foundation of reliable architecture data. The absence of violations demonstrates that the baseline architecture model is well-formed and that the catalogue update processes have preserved consistency across the interconnected catalogues.

proponent-analysis.finding: The CCaaS initiative **directly advances two core business strategies**: `BUS-STR-001` (operate as a customer-centric organisation) and `APP-STR-002` (buy commodity, build only where it differentiates). Contact centre management is commodity capability; acquiring CCaaS rather than building internally demonstrates disciplined portfolio stewardship and removes technical debt from a non-strategic system.
proponent-analysis.impact: Implementing CCaaS frees engineering capacity for competitive differentiation, reduces on-premises support burden on an unsupported legacy VOIP system, and enables the organisation to meet its target of reducing custom-build share below 40% by 2027. Strategic alignment strengthens the business case for investment priority and vendor funding.
proponent-analysis.recommendation: **Proceed with vendor selection.** Prioritise cloud-native CCaaS platforms aligned with `APP-STR-001` (cloud-native first) and evaluate vendors explicitly against the criterion of commodity interchangeability — avoid proprietary deployment models or vendor lock-in that would limit future replacement.
proponent-analysis.rationale: Strategic buy-in is critical for funding and execution. The CCaaS initiative is not a technology refresh; it is a strategic capability enabler that removes a barrier to customer-centric operations and allows engineering to focus on differentiating capabilities.

proponent-analysis.finding: The decision advances **Integration Architecture Strategy** (`INT-STR-001`, `INT-STR-003`, `INT-STR-005`) by establishing new inter-system exchanges with CRM and work planning. If designed as managed, versioned APIs with contract-first principles, the CCaaS platform becomes a reusable capability that supports future customer engagement initiatives and prevents integration debt.
proponent-analysis.impact: Integration debt currently constrains 40% of new-initiative effort. A contract-first approach to CCaaS integrations prevents tight coupling, enables future CCaaS vendor replacement without rewriting consuming systems, and positions contact centre capabilities as a composable, reusable service. This directly supports the organisation's drive to reduce integration friction.
proponent-analysis.recommendation: **Proceed with vendor selection — conditioned on defining integration contracts first.** Define API contracts between CCaaS and CRM, and between CCaaS and work planning, in the **Interface Catalogue** (`INT-IFC`) **before** vendor selection. Use these contracts to evaluate vendors, and reject vendors whose APIs do not align with the contracted schema. This ensures the integration is organisation-driven, not vendor-driven.
proponent-analysis.rationale: Contract-first design is the foundation of vendor portability and loose coupling. By establishing integration contracts upfront, the organisation retains control over the integration shape and decouples from vendor-specific concerns. This is essential for a long-term capability where vendor replacement may be necessary.

proponent-analysis.finding: The decision **removes a barrier to achieving critical business outcomes**: enabling 90% of frontline staff to operate in cross-functional customer-facing teams by end of 2027. The CCaaS platform's omnichannel capability (phone, email, chat, SMS) is an enabling technology for the customer-centric operating model the business is pursuing.
proponent-analysis.impact: Implementing CCaaS directly enables the business strategy of customer-centric operations and is a prerequisite for achieving the NPS improvement and cross-functional team target. Delaying CCaaS delays the ability to operate the target customer engagement model. The platform is an enabling capability, not a cost centre.
proponent-analysis.recommendation: **Proceed with high priority.** Link the CCaaS initiative explicitly to the 2027 frontline team target in the investment business case. Confirm with business sponsors that the omnichannel capability set (phone, email, chat, SMS) aligns with the channels they expect frontline staff to operate through. Use this alignment to justify investment priority relative to other initiatives.
proponent-analysis.rationale: Business outcomes provide the strongest justification for architecture investment. The CCaaS platform is not a technology initiative; it is a business capability enabler. Linking it to a named, time-bound outcome (90% cross-functional teams by 2027) elevates the decision and strengthens the case for funding and talent allocation.

proponent-analysis.finding: The decision has clear **architecture principles alignment** on core dimensions: cloud-native design (`APP-STR-001`), composability via stable APIs (`APP-PRN-002`), and contract-first integration design (`INT-PRN-002`). If vendor selection prioritises cloud-native platforms and API-first design, the CCaaS platform will integrate cleanly into the organisation's evolving application landscape.
proponent-analysis.impact: A cloud-native, API-first CCaaS platform aligns with the organisation's baseline expectations for observability, continuous deployment, and platform portability. This alignment reduces operational friction, enables standard observability practices (`APP-PRN-005`), and positions the platform as a long-term, maintainable capability rather than a technical liability.
proponent-analysis.recommendation: **Proceed with vendor selection — conditioned on architecture principles alignment.** During vendor evaluation, confirm that the CCaaS platform is cloud-native (containers, immutable infrastructure, declarative deployment) and exposes standard observability (logs, metrics, traces). If the vendor platform does not meet these expectations, explicitly acknowledge the divergence and document a mitigation strategy (e.g. wrapper containerisation).
proponent-analysis.rationale: Architecture principles are the contracts for technical quality. A CCaaS platform that aligns with cloud-native and observability principles will integrate into the operational landscape without creating new technical debt. A platform that violates these principles will require custom integration and become a long-term operational liability.

proponent-analysis.finding: The decision generates **valuable new data assets** that should be managed as products per `DAT-STR-001` (treat data as a product). Contact centre interactions, agent availability, and queue state are valuable signals for business analytics, customer journey analysis, and operational decision-making. CCaaS produces these assets at scale; managing them as formal data products unlocks cross-domain analytics value.
proponent-analysis.impact: Contact centre data is a strategic asset for understanding customer experience, identifying journey friction, and optimising operations. Treating CCaaS-generated data as a formal product (with named ownership, canonical definitions, and published access) positions the organisation to use this data for competitive advantage. Shadow analytics and custom pipelines (the alternative) waste engineering effort and fragment insights.
proponent-analysis.recommendation: **Proceed with vendor selection.** Define which entities the CCaaS platform will publish as data products (e.g. 'contact centre interaction records', 'queue state', 'agent availability') and assign named ownership in the **Data Domains & Concepts** (`DAT-DAC`) catalogue before implementation. Ensure the CRM and work planning integrations are documented as data product consumers, and confirm the chosen vendor supports data-as-a-product practices (classification, ownership, access control).
proponent-analysis.rationale: Data products are the foundation of trustworthy cross-domain analysis. By committing contact centre data to the data-as-product model, the organisation unlocks value that would otherwise be locked inside the CCaaS platform or replicated in shadow systems. This is a multiplier on the value of the CCaaS investment.

challenger-analysis.finding: **All governance guardrails are undefined.** Business, Application, Integration, and Data Guardrails catalogues are empty. The decision cannot be validated against organisation-level constraints on compliance, vendor lock-in, operational resilience, or privacy before proceeding. This creates material risk that the CCaaS platform will be selected and implemented without explicitly addressing business-critical constraints.
challenger-analysis.impact: Without guardrails, the organisation lacks enforcement points for regulatory compliance (GDPR, CCPA), data residency, vendor selection criteria, operational SLAs, or integration standards. A vendor platform selected without these guardrails may violate unstated compliance or operational expectations, requiring expensive post-implementation remediation or replacement.
challenger-analysis.recommendation: **Do not proceed to vendor selection until guardrails are defined.** Populate BUS-GRD, APP-GRD, INT-GRD, and DAT-GRD catalogues with guardrails relevant to CCaaS (data residency, observability standards, vendor lock-in, incident response SLAs, privacy controls). Once defined, validate this decision and any candidate vendors against them before committing.
challenger-analysis.rationale: Guardrails are the organisation's top-level control framework. A CCaaS platform that handles customer personal data and integrates with critical systems (CRM, work planning) must be evaluated against explicit guardrails. Proceeding without them trades short-term speed for long-term compliance and operational risk.

challenger-analysis.finding: **Business scope is underspecified.** The narrative states the platform will 'cover all digital platforms and channels' and 'drive customer engagement' but does not enumerate which channels (phone, email, chat, SMS, social), which customer segments are in scope, or map these to business capabilities in the Business Capabilities (`BUS-CAP`) catalogue. Requirements array is empty.
challenger-analysis.impact: Without clear scope boundaries and linked requirements, architecture analysis cannot validate whether the CCaaS platform addresses the stated business problem. This creates risk of scope creep during implementation, misalignment between business expectations and delivered capabilities, and inability to measure whether the platform achieves the stated strategic goal of 'customer-centric operations'.
challenger-analysis.recommendation: **Defer vendor selection until business scope is locked.** With business stakeholders, enumerate the channels, customer segments, and business capabilities in scope (e.g. 'Support phone, email, chat for customer support and sales teams'). Link these to entries in the Business Capabilities catalogue. Translate scope into measurable requirements (e.g. 'Support 500 concurrent users', 'Omnichannel routing within 3 seconds'). Add requirements to the decision JSON before proceeding.
challenger-analysis.rationale: Scope is the contract between business and delivery. Proceeding without locked scope invites scope creep, which is the leading cause of overruns in platform implementations. Clear scope boundaries also enable objective evaluation of whether the chosen vendor meets the business need.

challenger-analysis.finding: **Critical architecture decisions are deferred to post-vendor-selection.** The narrative does not define integration contracts (CCaaS ↔ CRM, CCaaS ↔ work planning), data ownership, privacy controls, or cloud-native operating model alignment. Proponent Analysis recommends 'contract-first' design before vendor selection, but this step is missing — vendor evaluation will be driven by what vendors offer, not what the organisation needs.
challenger-analysis.impact: If integration contracts are not defined before vendor selection, the chosen vendor's API shape will become the de facto integration contract, locking the organisation into vendor-specific models. Replacing the vendor later will require rewriting consuming systems. Similarly, undefined data ownership and privacy controls create risk that contact centre data will not be managed as a product per strategy (`DAT-STR-001`), and privacy compliance will be reactive rather than designed in.
challenger-analysis.recommendation: **Before vendor selection:** (1) Define integration contracts in the Interface Catalogue (`INT-IFC`) for CCaaS ↔ CRM and CCaaS ↔ work planning (OpenAPI 3.0 for synchronous APIs). (2) Define contact centre data entities in Data Domains & Concepts (`DAT-DAC`) with named ownership. (3) Confirm in the narrative that selected vendors will align to these contracts, not the reverse. (4) Lock cloud-native, observability, and twelve-factor principles as non-negotiable vendor requirements.
challenger-analysis.rationale: Contract-first design is the foundation of vendor portability. If contracts are deferred, the organisation yields control over integration design to the vendor, creating long-term coupling. This is particularly material for a platform that will handle customer personal data and integrate with business-critical systems.

challenger-analysis.finding: **Data ownership and governance are undefined.** The narrative does not name a steward for contact centre data (interaction records, queue state, agent availability) that the CCaaS platform will produce. Data Principles (`DAT-PRN-001`, `DAT-PRN-002`) require that every data domain has an owner and that definitions are canonical. The decision is silent on how contact centre data will be managed — as a formal data product or as proprietary to the CCaaS platform.
challenger-analysis.impact: Without named ownership, contact centre data governance is diffuse. Data quality issues, definition drift, and lifecycle decisions (retention, deletion, access control) will lack accountability. Additionally, if contact centre data is not canonically defined in the Data Domains & Concepts catalogue before CCaaS implementation, the vendor's internal data model will become the de facto definition, making it harder to integrate with CRM, work planning, or analytics platforms later.
challenger-analysis.recommendation: Before CCaaS implementation: (1) Identify and name the data steward (e.g. 'Contact Centre Operations Manager') responsible for contact centre data. (2) Review the Data Domains & Concepts catalogue for existing definitions of entities like 'Customer Interaction', 'Agent', 'Queue'; if they exist, ensure CCaaS aligns with them. If not, add canonical definitions to DAT-DAC with the named steward. (3) Confirm in vendor evaluation that the chosen platform supports data classification, ownership tracking, and access control per the data steward's governance model.
challenger-analysis.rationale: Data ownership is the precondition for trustworthy data. Contact centre data is a strategic asset (per Proponent Analysis); managing it as a formal product ensures it supports business analytics and cross-domain decision-making rather than remaining locked in the CCaaS platform or duplicated in shadow systems.

challenger-analysis.finding: **Operational principles are not locked in vendor evaluation.** The Principles Alignment section identifies that Application Principles (`APP-PRN-001`: twelve-factor, `APP-PRN-005`: observability) and Integration Principles (`INT-PRN-002`: contracts-first, `INT-PRN-006`: boundary translation) are silent or at risk. The narrative does not confirm that vendor selection will enforce these principles as non-negotiable requirements — it is possible the chosen vendor will not support twelve-factor patterns, standard observability, or API contract versioning.
challenger-analysis.impact: If the selected vendor does not meet operational principles expectations (e.g. requires vendor-proprietary deployment, exposes vendor-internal data models directly to integrations, provides only proprietary observability), the CCaaS platform will diverge from the baseline and create long-term operational friction. Operations teams will lack visibility into CCaaS performance; integrations will leak vendor concerns into the organisation's landscape; and the platform will be harder to replace if vendor needs change.
challenger-analysis.recommendation: In the ADR narrative, explicitly state that vendor selection will enforce: (1) Cloud-native deployment (containers, immutable infrastructure, declarative config), (2) Twelve-factor compliance (config via environment, stateless processes, stdout logging), (3) Standard observability (OpenTelemetry-compatible logs, metrics, traces), (4) API-first design with versioned, managed APIs. Document these as evaluation criteria; reject vendors that do not meet them or require workarounds.
challenger-analysis.rationale: Operational principles are the contracts for technical quality. A CCaaS platform that violates baseline expectations (cloud-native, observable, composable) will require custom integration for observability and will become a long-term operational liability. Locking these principles into vendor evaluation upfront prevents expensive post-implementation remediation.

Ensure the entry captures the cloud-based contact centre platform that replaces the legacy on-premises VOIP system.
